solution:
(a) ENERGY OF A PHOTON:
\(E = h\nu = 6{\cdot}626 \times 10^{-34} \times 6{\cdot}4 \times 10^{14} = 42{\cdot}41 \times 10^{-20}\ \mathrm{J}\)
Converting to electronvolts by dividing by \(1{\cdot}6 \times 10^{-19}\):
\(E = 2{\cdot}65\ \mathrm{eV}\)
(b) MAXIMUM KINETIC ENERGY, from Einstein's photoelectric equation:
\(K_{max} = E - \phi_{0} = 2{\cdot}65 - 1{\cdot}96 = 0{\cdot}69\ \mathrm{eV}\)
that is \(1{\cdot}10 \times 10^{-19}\) J. The emission is possible because the photon energy exceeds the work function; had it not, no electron would have been emitted however intense the light.
(c) STOPPING POTENTIAL. The stopping potential is the retarding voltage that just turns back the fastest electron, so the work done against it equals that electron's kinetic energy:
\(eV_{0} = K_{max} \quad\Longrightarrow\quad V_{0} = \dfrac{K_{max}}{e}\)
Working in electronvolts makes this immediate: a kinetic energy of \(0{\cdot}69\) eV is by definition the energy an electron gains through \(0{\cdot}69\) V, so
\(V_{0} = 0{\cdot}69\ \mathrm{V}\)
The numerical equality of \(K_{max}\) in electronvolts and \(V_{0}\) in volts is not a coincidence but the definition of the electronvolt, and it is the quickest check on this kind of answer.
note: 6.626 x 6.4 = 42.41, printed 42.24; carried through: E 2.65 eV, Kmax 0.69 eV = 1.10e-19 J, V0 0.69 V.

solution:
(a) The WORK FUNCTION of a metal is the MINIMUM energy required to free an electron from its surface, that is to remove it from the metal against the attraction of the ions left behind.
DETERMINING IT FROM THE GRAPH. Einstein's equation written in terms of the stopping potential is
\(eV_{0} = h\nu - \phi_{0} \quad\Longrightarrow\quad V_{0} = \dfrac{h}{e}\nu - \dfrac{\phi_{0}}{e}\)
which is a straight line of the form \(y = mx + c\). Plotting \(V_{0}\) against \(\nu\) therefore gives a straight line whose INTERCEPT ON THE VERTICAL AXIS is \(-\dfrac{\phi_{0}}{e}\), so
\(\phi_{0} = e \times \left|\text{intercept on the } V_{0}\text{ axis}\right|\)
Equivalently, the line cuts the frequency axis at the threshold frequency \(\nu_{0}\), and \(\phi_{0} = h\nu_{0}\), so the work function can be read from either intercept. The SLOPE, being \(\dfrac{h}{e}\), is the same for every metal and carries no information about the work function.
(b) Using the same equation with \(V_{0} = 0{\cdot}6\) V and \(\phi_{0} = 2{\cdot}4\) eV, working throughout in electronvolts:
\(eV_{0} = \dfrac{hc}{\lambda} - \phi_{0}\)
\(0{\cdot}6 = \dfrac{hc}{\lambda} - 2{\cdot}4 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \dfrac{hc}{\lambda} = 3{\cdot}0\ \mathrm{eV}\)
With \(hc = 1241\ \mathrm{eV\,nm}\):
\(\lambda = \dfrac{1241}{3{\cdot}0} = 413{\cdot}7\ \mathrm{nm}\)
The wavelength of the light used is about 414 nm, in the violet.

**(a) The speed.**

The de Broglie relation ties wavelength to momentum:

\(\lambda = \dfrac{h}{mv} \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad v = \dfrac{h}{m\lambda}\)

With \(\lambda = 0{\cdot}30\ \mathrm{nm} = 3{\cdot}0 \times 10^{-10}\ \mathrm{m}\), \(h = 6{\cdot}63 \times 10^{-34}\ \mathrm{J\,s}\) and \(m = 9{\cdot}1 \times 10^{-31}\ \mathrm{kg}\):

\(v = \dfrac{6{\cdot}63 \times 10^{-34}}{9{\cdot}1 \times 10^{-31} \times 3{\cdot}0 \times 10^{-10}} = \dfrac{6{\cdot}63 \times 10^{-34}}{2{\cdot}73 \times 10^{-40}}\)

\(v = 2{\cdot}43 \times 10^{6}\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\)

**(b) The kinetic energy.**

\(K = \tfrac{1}{2}mv^{2} = \tfrac{1}{2} \times 9{\cdot}1 \times 10^{-31} \times (2{\cdot}43 \times 10^{6})^{2}\)

\(K = 2{\cdot}69 \times 10^{-18}\ \mathrm{J}\)

Converting, with \(1\ \mathrm{eV} = 1{\cdot}6 \times 10^{-19}\ \mathrm{J}\):

\(K = \dfrac{2{\cdot}69 \times 10^{-18}}{1{\cdot}6 \times 10^{-19}} \approx 16{\cdot}8\ \mathrm{eV}\)

**A cleaner route to (b).** Eliminating \(v\) between the two relations gives the kinetic energy straight from the wavelength:

\(K = \dfrac{h^{2}}{2m\lambda^{2}}\)

Substituting the same numbers returns \(16{\cdot}8\) eV, which is a genuine check rather than a repetition: it never passes through the rounded value of \(v\), so agreement confirms the intermediate step.

The published scheme carries \(v = 2{\cdot}41 \times 10^{6}\) m/s at this point and \(16{\cdot}5\) eV at the end. Dividing \(6{\cdot}63\) by \(2{\cdot}73\) gives \(2{\cdot}4286\), so the intended figures are \(2{\cdot}43 \times 10^{6}\) m/s and \(16{\cdot}8\) eV; the gap is a rounding slip of under two per cent and changes nothing about the method.

**Worth noticing.** An electron of this wavelength is well inside the non-relativistic regime (\(v\) is under one per cent of \(c\)), so \(K = \tfrac{1}{2}mv^{2}\) is safe here. And \(0{\cdot}30\) nm is about the spacing of atoms in a crystal, which is exactly why electrons of a few tens of electronvolts diffract from crystals and why the Davisson-Germer experiment worked at these energies.

CBSE's marking scheme:

\(\lambda = \dfrac{h}{\sqrt{2m\mathrm{K}}}\)

\(\mathrm{K} = \left(\dfrac{500}{1{\cdot}673}\right)\mathrm{eV} = \dfrac{500\times 1{\cdot}6\times 10^{-19}}{1{\cdot}673}\ \mathrm{J}\)

\(\lambda_p = \dfrac{6{\cdot}63\times 10^{-34}}{\sqrt{2\times 1{\cdot}673\times 10^{-27}\times\left(\dfrac{500\times 1{\cdot}6\times 10^{-19}}{1{\cdot}673}\right)}} = 1{\cdot}65\times 10^{-12}\ \mathrm{m}\)

\(\lambda\propto\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{m}}\)

For an \(\alpha\) particle, \(m_\alpha = 4m_p\), and therefore

\(\lambda_\alpha = \dfrac{\lambda_p}{2}\)

Marks: ½ for the formula, ½ for the energy in joules, ½ for the substitution, ½ for the value, ½ for the mass dependence, ½ for the result.

Added here, and not from the marking scheme: the awkward-looking energy \(\left(500/1{\cdot}673\right)\mathrm{eV}\) is chosen precisely so that the \(1{\cdot}673\) cancels the proton mass. Under the root,

\(2\times\left(1{\cdot}673\times 10^{-27}\right)\times\dfrac{500\times 1{\cdot}6\times 10^{-19}}{1{\cdot}673} = 2\times 10^{-27}\times 500\times 1{\cdot}6\times 10^{-19} = 1{\cdot}6\times 10^{-43}\)

whose square root is exactly \(4{\cdot}0\times 10^{-22}\ \mathrm{kg\,m\,s^{-1}}\), leaving \(\lambda = \dfrac{6{\cdot}63\times 10^{-34}}{4{\cdot}0\times 10^{-22}}\), which is \(1{\cdot}66\times 10^{-12}\ \mathrm{m}\) (the scheme's \(1{\cdot}65\) cuts off \(1{\cdot}6575\)).

For the second part, note that \(\lambda = h/\sqrt{2m\mathrm{K}}\) contains the mass and the kinetic energy but NOT the charge, so the alpha particle's doubled charge plays no part whatever. Its wavelength is halved purely because its mass is four times that of the proton, and \(\sqrt{4} = 2\).

**"Second excited state" means \(n = 3\)**: the ground state is \(n = 1\), the first excited state \(n = 2\). Getting this wrong makes everything else wrong, and it is the only place in this question where a mark is really at risk.

**Step 1: the energy of that state.**

\(E_n = -\dfrac{13{\cdot}6}{n^{2}}\ \mathrm{eV} \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad E_3 = -\dfrac{13{\cdot}6}{9} = -1{\cdot}51\ \mathrm{eV}\)

**Step 2: the KINETIC energy.** For a bound state in a Coulomb field, the kinetic energy is the magnitude of the total energy:

\(K = -E = +1{\cdot}51\ \mathrm{eV}\)

**This step is the physics of the question.** The de Broglie wavelength needs **momentum**, so the **total** energy, which is negative and includes the potential term, cannot be used directly. The virial result \(K = -E\) is what converts one into the other.

**In joules:**

\(K = 1{\cdot}51 \times 1{\cdot}6\times 10^{-19} = 2{\cdot}42\times 10^{-19}\ \mathrm{J}\)

**Step 3: the de Broglie wavelength.**

\(\lambda = \dfrac{h}{p} = \dfrac{h}{\sqrt{2mK}}\)

\(2mK = 2\left(9\times 10^{-31}\right)\left(2{\cdot}42\times 10^{-19}\right) = 4{\cdot}36\times 10^{-49}\)

\(\sqrt{2mK} = 6{\cdot}60\times 10^{-25}\ \mathrm{kg\,m\,s^{-1}}\)

\(\lambda = \dfrac{6{\cdot}6\times 10^{-34}}{6{\cdot}60\times 10^{-25}}\)

\(\boxed{\ \lambda \approx 1 \times 10^{-9}\ \mathrm{m} = 1\ \mathrm{nm}\ }\)

**An independent check from Bohr's own postulate**, which is worth doing because it uses none of the same numbers. The quantisation condition \(mvr = nh/2\pi\) can be rewritten

\(2\pi r_n = n\lambda\)

That is, the orbit's circumference is a whole number of de Broglie wavelengths. With \(r_3 = 9a_0 = 9\times 0{\cdot}529\times 10^{-10} = 4{\cdot}76\times 10^{-10}\) m:

\(\lambda = \dfrac{2\pi\left(4{\cdot}76\times 10^{-10}\right)}{3} = 9{\cdot}97\times 10^{-10}\ \mathrm{m}\ \checkmark\)

**The two routes agree to better than half a percent**, and the second is the more illuminating: it shows that **the electron in the \(n^{th}\) orbit fits exactly \(n\) of its own wavelengths around the circumference.** Three, here.

**That is what Bohr's quantisation MEANS.** His condition on angular momentum looked arbitrary in 1913; de Broglie's 1924 insight recast it as a **standing wave**: the orbits that survive are those where the electron's wave closes on itself in phase, and any other radius would have the wave interfere with itself destructively and vanish.

**A note on the arithmetic.** With the rounded constants supplied, the answer lands on \(1{\cdot}00\) nm almost exactly. That tidiness is a property of the numbers chosen, not a physical coincidence worth reading into.

**The answer is (B): \(6{\cdot}0 \times 10^{-20}\) J.**

**The photon's energy.**

\(E = \dfrac{hc}{\lambda} = \dfrac{6{\cdot}63 \times 10^{-34} \times 3 \times 10^{8}}{663 \times 10^{-9}}\)

\(E = \dfrac{1{\cdot}989 \times 10^{-25}}{6{\cdot}63 \times 10^{-7}} = 3{\cdot}0 \times 10^{-19}\ \mathrm{J}\)

The numbers are chosen so that 663 divides 6.63 exactly, worth spotting, since it turns the division into a shift of the exponent.

**The work function, in the same units.**

\(\phi_0 = 1{\cdot}50\ \mathrm{eV} = 1{\cdot}50 \times 1{\cdot}6 \times 10^{-19} = 2{\cdot}4 \times 10^{-19}\ \mathrm{J}\)

This conversion is the step the question is really testing: the photon energy comes out in joules and the work function is given in electronvolts, and the two cannot be subtracted until they agree. All four options are in joules, so the answer must be too.

**Einstein's photoelectric equation.**

\(K_{\max} = E - \phi_0 = (3{\cdot}0 - 2{\cdot}4) \times 10^{-19} = 0{\cdot}6 \times 10^{-19}\)

\(K_{\max} = 6{\cdot}0 \times 10^{-20}\ \mathrm{J}\)

**A check in electronvolts.** \(E = 3{\cdot}0 \times 10^{-19}/1{\cdot}6 \times 10^{-19} = 1{\cdot}875\) eV, so \(K_{\max} = 1{\cdot}875 - 1{\cdot}50 = 0{\cdot}375\) eV, and \(0{\cdot}375 \times 1{\cdot}6 \times 10^{-19} = 6{\cdot}0 \times 10^{-20}\) J. The two routes agree.

Note that the photon energy exceeds the work function by only a quarter of an electronvolt, so this red light (663 nm) is barely above the threshold for this metal, whose threshold wavelength is about \(8290\ \mathring{\mathrm{A}}\), in the near infrared.

**The answer is (A): \(10^{16}\).**

**Step 1: the energy of one photon.**

\(E = h\nu = 6{\cdot}63 \times 10^{-34} \times 5{\cdot}0 \times 10^{14} = 3{\cdot}315 \times 10^{-19}\ \mathrm{J}\)

**Step 2: the energy emitted each second.** Power is energy per second, so in one second the source emits

\(P = 3{\cdot}31\ \mathrm{mW} = 3{\cdot}31 \times 10^{-3}\ \mathrm{J\,s^{-1}}\)

**Step 3: divide.**

\(n = \dfrac{P}{E} = \dfrac{3{\cdot}31 \times 10^{-3}}{3{\cdot}315 \times 10^{-19}}\)

\(\boxed{\ n \approx 1 \times 10^{16}\ \text{photons per second}\ }\)

**The numbers are chosen so the mantissas cancel.** \(3{\cdot}31\) and \(3{\cdot}315\) agree to three figures, so the whole calculation collapses to \(10^{-3}/10^{-19} = 10^{16}\) and the options (all bare powers of ten) confirm that only the exponent is being tested. Subtracting the exponents is the entire arithmetic.

**Checking against the options by size.** \(10^{24}\) would be about a million times Avogadro's number of photons a second from a milliwatt source, which is absurd. \(10^{10}\) would mean each photon carried \(10^{-13}\) J, about a million electronvolts, a gamma ray, not visible light. Only \(10^{16}\) is consistent with a millwatt of optical radiation.

**What the number means, and it is the point of the question.** Ten thousand million million photons leave this source every second. **The graininess of light is completely invisible at ordinary intensities**: the arrival of photons is so rapid and so dense that the beam appears perfectly smooth and continuous, which is why the wave picture served so well for so long.

**The frequency identifies the light.** \(5{\cdot}0 \times 10^{14}\) Hz corresponds to

\(\lambda = \dfrac{c}{\nu} = \dfrac{3 \times 10^{8}}{5 \times 10^{14}} = 6 \times 10^{-7}\ \mathrm{m} = 600\ \mathrm{nm}\)

which is orange light, and each of its photons carries about \(2{\cdot}1\) eV.
note: Power is J per second; printed J.
